name: Su-57 Felon
tagline: Russia's twin-engine answer to the F-22 and F-35. It combines low-observable shaping, internal weapons bays and supercruise performance, though independent analysts judge its radar cross-section and production numbers to trail well behind its American rivals.
history: The Su-57 grew out of Russia's PAK FA (Perspective Aviation Complex of Frontline Aviation) programme launched in the 2000s to replace the MiG-29 and Su-27 with a genuine stealth fighter. The T-50 prototype first flew on 29 January 2010, and after a long, sanctions-slowed development the type - renamed Su-57 - entered serial production in 2019 and formally joined Russian Aerospace Forces service in December 2020. Early production was tiny, hampered by the loss of Ukrainian-sourced components after 2014 and by a fatal 2019 prototype crash, but output has since increased at the Komsomolsk-on-Amur plant. The Su-57 has flown in the war against Ukraine since shortly after the February 2022 invasion, initially launching missiles from within Russian airspace before later flights - escorted by Su-35s - fired Kh-59/Kh-69 stand-off cruise missiles at Ukrainian targets; Russian officials have also claimed unconfirmed air-to-air kills for the type. In June 2024 Ukraine claimed a long-range drone strike damaged or destroyed Su-57s at Akhtubinsk air base, illustrating the aircraft's continued vulnerability even far from the front line. In 2025-2026 Algeria became the Su-57's first confirmed export customer, taking delivery of Su-57E variants and making the type's combat debut outside Russian service a live possibility for the years ahead.

specifications.cruiseSpeed: Mach 1.3 supercruise (sustained supersonic flight without afterburner)

range.text: 2,175 mi (3,500 km) on internal fuel; extended further with aerial refuelling via retractable probe

specifications.weight: empty: 40,785 lb (18,500 kg); normal takeoff: 55,115 lb (25,000 kg); MTOW: 77,160 lb (35,000 kg)
specifications.engines: 2 x Saturn AL-41F1 (izdeliye 117) turbofans, ~142 kN afterburning thrust each; later production shifting to the more powerful izdeliye 30 (AL-51F1)
specifications.armament: 1 x GSh-30-1 30mm cannon (150 rounds); internal bays for R-77M/R-37M air-to-air missiles and Kh-38/Kh-59MK2/Kh-69 stand-off missiles or KAB-250/500 guided bombs; 6 external hardpoints for non-stealth missions
specifications.capacity: N/A - single-seat fighter; internal bays carry ~1,500 kg (3,300 lb), rising to ~10,000 kg (22,000 lb) total with external hardpoints in non-stealth loadouts

unitCost.text: ~$35-42M (officially cited figure); Western analysts believe true program unit cost is considerably higher given low-rate production

variants.desc: Baseline production fighter for the Russian Aerospace Forces, following the T-50 prototype programme.
Upgraded production standard re-engined with the more powerful izdeliye 30 (AL-51F1) turbofan.
Export configuration with modified IFF and export-cleared systems; first delivered to Algeria from 2025.
Related lightweight single-engine stealth fighter concept developed alongside the Su-57 for export markets, not a direct variant.

flightradar24.howToFind: Su-57s essentially never broadcast civil ADS-B and rarely leave Russian or, now, Algerian airspace, so confirmed Flightradar24 sightings are effectively unheard of; most public tracking of the type instead comes from geolocated video, satellite imagery of Akhtubinsk and Lipetsk, and air-show flypasts such as MAKS.

quickFacts: Russia's first stealth fighter has been built in tiny numbers - Western estimates suggest only a few dozen delivered, fewer than China builds of the J-20 in a year.
In June 2024, Ukrainian drones struck Akhtubinsk airbase and damaged at least one Su-57 on the ground - the first stealth fighter ever damaged by enemy action.
Algeria became the type's first export customer, with deliveries reported from 2025.
It has flown combat missions over Ukraine mostly as a stand-off missile launcher, rarely crossing the front line.
The first production aircraft crashed before delivery in 2019 - an inauspicious start for the program.
Its 3D thrust-vectoring makes it arguably the most agile fighter flying - at airshows it performs manoeuvres no Western stealth jet attempts.

overview: The Sukhoi Su-57 is a Russian twin-engine stealth fighter developed by Sukhoi for the Russian Aerospace Forces. It first flew in 2010 and carries its weapons internally in tandem belly bays to reduce radar signature.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

Production has run well behind plan - only a few dozen of a planned 76 aircraft were in service by the mid-2020s. It has flown combat missions over Ukraine from stand-off range since 2022, and Algeria became its first export customer, receiving initial Su-57Es in early 2026.{{ref:twz-algeria}}

sections.heading: Origins & Concept
paragraphs: The PAK FA program of the early 2000s set out to give Russia what the F-22 had given America: a fifth-generation air-superiority fighter combining stealth, supercruise, sensor fusion and super-manoeuvrability. Sukhoi's T-50 design won the assignment, flying first on 29 January 2010 from Komsomolsk-on-Amur.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

The philosophy diverged deliberately from Lockheed's: where the F-22 buys survivability almost entirely through signature, the T-50 blended moderate stealth with extreme agility - 3D thrust-vectoring nozzles, relaxed stability, enormous control authority - betting that a fighter which is hard to see AND nearly impossible to out-turn beats one optimised for either alone.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

India joined as co-developer in 2007 with plans for a two-seat FGFA derivative, then withdrew in 2018 citing cost, technology-sharing and stealth-performance concerns - a loss of funding and scale from which the program's economics never fully recovered.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

sections.heading: Design & Engineering
paragraphs: The Felon's airframe is a widescreen blend of Flanker heritage and stealth shaping: widely spaced engines with a lifting body between them, all-moving tail surfaces, serrated skins and S-shaped(ish) inlets, and two tandem internal bays sized for its principal air-to-air and cruise missiles, with wing-root bays for short-range weapons. Western assessments generally credit a real but partial signature reduction - well above Flanker, short of F-22/F-35 class.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

Its sensor suite is ambitious: the N036 Byelka radar spreads five AESA arrays around the airframe (including side-looking and L-band wing arrays aimed at counter-stealth), paired with an infrared search-and-track ball and a heavily automated cockpit. The intended second-stage AL-51 'izdeliye 30' engines - promising supercruise and serrated stealth nozzles - began flying on production aircraft only in the mid-2020s, years behind schedule.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

sections.heading: Service History
paragraphs: Deliveries tell the program's story: a 2019 order for 76 aircraft by 2028, first serial delivery in 2020 (after the very first production jet crashed pre-delivery in 2019), and a trickle thereafter - Western estimates put the operational fleet in the dozens by the mid-2020s, with 2025's deliveries to the VKS reported as minimal while export airframes took priority.{{ref:ni-deliveries}}

Over Ukraine the Su-57 has flown combat missions since 2022 - launching stand-off missiles from Russian airspace and reportedly conducting some defence-suppression sorties - while Moscow keeps its rarest fighter carefully clear of contested airspace. Ukrainian long-range drone strikes claimed damage to at least one Felon at Akhtubinsk in 2024, underlining why: each airframe is, effectively, irreplaceable in the near term.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

The export breakthrough came late but concretely: Algeria confirmed itself as launch customer in early 2025{{ref:mwm-algeria}}, with a reported 2021-vintage contract for 14 Su-57Es - roughly six delivered from 2025, footage confirming operations alongside Algerian Su-35s by February 2026 - and India, post-2025 border tensions, publicly re-examining the type it once abandoned.{{ref:twz-algeria}}{{ref:aer-algeria}}

sections.heading: Development
paragraphs: The program's second decade is about volume and derivatives: a modernised Su-57M with the definitive engines, the single-engine Su-75 'Checkmate' pitched as its affordable stablemate (still unflown years after its 2021 rollout), and teaming trials with the S-70 Okhotnik-B stealth combat drone - the Felon cast as command node for Russia's loyal-wingman ambitions.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

Sanctions run through everything: Western-sourced machine tools and electronics named in leaked documents, workarounds through third countries, and a production system visibly straining to scale. The Su-57's engineering is no longer its hardest problem; its industrial base is.{{ref:ni-deliveries}}

sections.heading: Current Status & Outlook
paragraphs: Verdicts on the Felon split along what you measure. As a technology demonstrator for Russian aerospace - vectoring stealth, distributed AESA, weapons-bay integration - it delivered genuine firsts for its industry. As a fleet, it has yet to matter: numbers too small to shape any campaign, held back from the one war its country is fighting.{{ref:wiki-su57}}

Its next decade will decide which reading holds: Algeria's jets entering full service, India's choice pending, engines finally maturing - or a small fleet overtaken by sixth-generation programmes already flying elsewhere.{{ref:twz-algeria}}

accidentsAndIncidents.title: First production Su-57 destroyed in test crash
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: The first serial-production Su-57 crashed and exploded on impact roughly 68 miles from the Komsomolsk-on-Amur plant, reportedly during a flight-control or engine-related test. The pilot ejected and was rescued alive.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Damaged by a Ukrainian drone strike
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: Ukraine's military intelligence said a drone strike hit an Su-57 at Akhtubinsk airfield, roughly 589 km from the front line. A Russian military-affiliated channel acknowledged shrapnel damage, though the full extent and repair status were unconfirmed.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Crash near Moscow amid suspected friendly fire
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: An Su-57 crashed near Zvenigorod, west of Moscow, during what Russia's defence ministry called a takeoff accident. Russian military bloggers suggested the capital's air-defence batteries may have shot it down, a cause Russian officials have not confirmed. The pilot ejected safely.
